title: One-time pads & block ciphers
blocks: Perfect secrecy, practical security, and DES
notes: Continue from last lecture’s repeating-key weaknesses. Today we contrast a proof of perfect secrecy with the structure and limitations of practical block ciphers.

title: From a repeating key to a one-time pad
blocks: Vigenère repeats a short key. Positions sharing one key letter form interleaved shift ciphers.
What if the key never repeats, is as long as the message, and is chosen uniformly at random?
The one-time pad removes the repeated schedule. Its security will follow from a precise probability argument.
notes: Connect to the previous lecture’s aligned-column attack. No new key schedule should be assumed random merely because it looks complicated. The next slide makes independence and uniformity explicit.

title: The requirements all matter
blocks: Every pad of the required length is equally likely; it is independent of the plaintext.
One fresh pad symbol for every plaintext symbol.
Only the parties know the pad; no pad segment is reused.
A deterministic expansion of a short secret does not supply a uniformly random pad of arbitrary length.
take: Perfect secrecy requires these assumptions, including an independent key and a single use.
notes: Treat the conditions as a mathematical model. A uniformly selected n-bit pad has 2^n equally likely values; a short seed has fewer possible expanded sequences. Explain that key independence rules out key generation correlated with message content.

title: A letter example: NANYANG with XRTRPLK
take: A = 0, …, Z = 25. The complete ciphertext is KRGPPYQ; decryption subtracts the pad modulo 26.
notes: Retains the original NANYANG / XRTRPLK illustration. Work the first row: N=13, X=23, 36 mod 26 = 10 = K. Point out the two different outputs for repeated N. The seven-letter row is illustrative; a real pad must actually satisfy the generation conditions.

title: For bits, addition modulo 2 is XOR
blocks: A bit is 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits. XOR applies separately at each position.
notes: Define the ⊕ symbol before using it in message equations. Bitwise XOR is x ^ y in Python, C, C++, and Java; MATLAB uses bitxor(x,y), and R uses bitwXor(x,y). Leading zeroes are part of the specified bit-string length.

title: The same XOR operation decrypts
blocks: Each bit is its own additive inverse modulo 2: adding it twice cancels it.
The identities apply bit by bit to equal-length strings, not just to a single bit.
notes: Use associativity of XOR to regroup terms. Over Z2, subtraction equals addition, so decryption can use the same operation. Distinguish a repeated operation from repeated pad use: applying the same key to decrypt its one ciphertext is correct.

title: Exercise: encrypt these ten bits
blocks: Compute the ciphertext one position at a time. Preserve the ten-bit length.
Then apply the same pad to your ciphertext and check that the plaintext returns.
notes: This is the original reference exercise. Pause before advancing to the answer. The first three XOR operations are 1⊕0=1, 0⊕1=1, 1⊕1=0.

title: Worked answer: encrypt, then reverse
blocks: Every ciphertext bit is computed from exactly one plaintext bit and one pad bit.
notes: Answer: 1100110110. Check several equal-bit and unequal-bit positions. Reinforce that XOR has no carries between positions; ordinary integer addition is a different operation.

title: Why a pad segment must never be reused
blocks: Suppose two messages p₁ and p₂ use the same pad k, producing ciphertexts c₁ and c₂.
An interceptor learns a relation between the plaintexts. Knowing one plaintext reveals the other.
take: Fresh key material is required for every message and every pad segment.
notes: A relation between plaintexts is already a confidentiality failure; reuse does not automatically reveal both messages in full. With structure or known plaintext, the relation can be exploited. Use the next ten-bit example to make cancellation visible.

title: Pad reuse: cancellation in an actual example
blocks: The attacker computes the last row directly from the two ciphertexts, without learning the pad first.
notes: Both messages here use pad 0110101110. The second ciphertext is 1010100011. The XOR relation is 0110010101. If p₁ is known, p₂ = p₁ ⊕ (c₁ ⊕ c₂). The example is an arithmetic illustration rather than a language-based reconstruction.

title: A historical lesson: VENONA
blocks: Some Soviet intelligence messages used codebooks with additive one-time-pad material.
Duplicate pad material caused some additives to be reused. VENONA analysts exploited this reuse together with message structure and other evidence.
The lesson is operational: the mathematical guarantee depends on how keys are generated, distributed, and consumed.
notes: Keep the claim limited: reused additives helped recover parts of messages; neither all Soviet traffic nor every reused-pad message was automatically solved. Do not portray this as breaking a correctly implemented one-time pad. Predictable additive sequences likewise violate the uniform-pad assumption.
source: Historical case: NSA/CSS, VENONA declassified history.

title: Simple operations, demanding key management
blocks: Early pads could be paper sheets destroyed after use; the name combines “one time” with that physical pad.
A 1 GB message requires 1 GB of fresh secret pad material, already shared securely. Storage, synchronization, and avoiding reuse dominate the logistics.
Historically, pads were useful in specialized diplomatic and intelligence communications. Their confidentiality claim does not by itself provide message authenticity.
notes: The byte count is a minimum fresh-pad length for the same binary message representation, before administrative overhead. Physical pads motivate deletion after use. The modern practical alternative is not a short “random-looking” pad called an OTP; later sections distinguish computational constructions.

title: Random variables and their probabilities
blocks: A discrete random variable X takes values x in a finite value space. Write Pr[X = x] for the probability of one value.
notes: Cryptographic plaintext, key, and ciphertext will be random variables. Lowercase letters denote possible values, not additional random variables. The fair coin is a distributional model, not a promise that every random quantity is uniform.

title: Joint probability and independence
blocks: For random variables X and Y, the joint probability Pr[X = x, Y = y] describes both values occurring together.
X and Y are independent precisely when the joint distribution factors for every pair of values:
notes: Independence is an assumption that must be justified, not a property implied by different variable names. It will be essential that the OTP key K is independent of the message P.

title: Two dice: define the observations first
blocks: Roll two fair, independent dice D₁ and D₂. Let X = D₁ + D₂. Let Y = d for a double and Y = n otherwise.
take: The 36 ordered die outcomes are equally likely. Sum 4 occurs at (1,3), (2,2), and (3,1).
notes: Use the 6×6 grid of ordered outcomes. Highlight all six diagonal outcomes as doubles and outline the three cells with sum 4; the intersection is (2,2). X ranges from 2 to 12, while Y takes only d or n. The observations X and Y need not be independent even though D₁ and D₂ are.

title: Conditioning: restrict the possible outcomes
blocks: The bar means “given”. Among the three outcomes with sum 4, exactly one is a double.
notes: State that the conditioning event must have positive probability. Compare 1/3 with the unconditioned double probability 1/6 to show X and Y are dependent. This also illustrates joint = conditional × marginal.

title: Bayes’ rule reverses the conditioning
blocks: For Pr[X = x] > 0 and Pr[Y = y] > 0, factor the same joint probability in either order:
In the dice example, ask for sum 4 after learning that a double occurred:
take: The two conditional probabilities differ, but each gives the same joint probability 1/36.
notes: The six doubles are equally likely and only (2,2) has sum 4, so direct counting also gives 1/6. Reversing the condition does not preserve its value. We will use Bayes to compare a plaintext prior with its ciphertext-conditioned posterior.

title: Perfect secrecy: observing c changes no belief
blocks: Let P denote the plaintext random variable and C the ciphertext random variable; p and c denote particular messages.
The right side is the prior probability. The left side is the posterior after observing c. Perfect secrecy makes them equal.
notes: This is independence of P and C. It does not assert that every plaintext has the same prior probability. The guarantee concerns the stated ciphertext observation and fixed message-length model, not arbitrary side information or authenticity.

title: Two bits: every plaintext has a compatible pad
blocks: Suppose the observed ciphertext is c = 10. For each candidate plaintext p, exactly one two-bit pad k = p ⊕ c produces it.
take: Equal-likelihood pads do not imply equal-likelihood plaintexts: the attacker retains the original prior.
notes: Rows should be p=00,k=10; p=01,k=11; p=10,k=00; p=11,k=01. Each pad has probability 1/4 and is independent of P. The diagram is intuition for a conditional likelihood argument, not a proof that the plaintext prior is uniform.

title: State the model for an n-bit proof
blocks: Let n be the fixed message length. Plaintext P, key K, and ciphertext C take values in the n-bit strings.
K is uniform and independent of P: every key k has probability 2⁻ⁿ. The distribution of P can be arbitrary.
notes: All variables and spaces are now explicit. Fixed length matters: the theorem does not promise to hide message length. Uniform n-bit K is independent of arbitrary P, including biased or partially predictable messages. Used-once and secrecy are the operational conditions for applying this one-message model.

title: Proof 1: a fixed message gives a uniform ciphertext
blocks: Fix a plaintext p with positive probability and any ciphertext c. The unique compatible pad is p ⊕ c.
Independence lets us ignore the condition P = p; uniformity makes this probability the same for every key.
notes: Separate the two assumptions: independence removes conditioning; uniformity gives 2^-n. Uniqueness follows from XOR cancellation. We condition only on positive-prior plaintexts, so no undefined conditional probability is used.

title: Proof 2: sum over the possible plaintexts
blocks: The law of total probability averages those identical likelihoods using the actual plaintext probabilities.
The ciphertext is uniform even when the plaintext is biased. The proof has not assumed a uniform message source.
notes: The sum is over the support of P, written explicitly to avoid conditioning on zero-probability values. Plaintext probabilities sum to 1, so every c has positive probability 2^-n. This supplies the denominator needed by Bayes.

title: Proof 3: the posterior equals the prior
blocks: For any plaintext p with positive prior probability, apply Bayes’ rule:
If p has prior probability zero, its joint probability with c is zero, so its posterior is also zero. This covers every plaintext.
take: The proof holds for every plaintext distribution under the stated independent, uniform-pad model.
notes: All c have positive probability by the previous page. Explicitly close the zero-prior case rather than claiming conditional likelihoods are defined there. Perfect secrecy is a theorem about distributions, not a claim that a computational attack happens to be slow.

title: A biased prior remains biased
blocks: The most likely plaintext remains 00. Perfect secrecy prevents the ciphertext from improving the attacker’s prior information.
notes: The ciphertext probability is 1/4 even for this nonuniform prior. For example, joint probability P=00,C=10 equals (1/2)(1/4)=1/8, so posterior is(1/8)/(1/4)=1/2. All plaintexts being compatible does not mean they become equally likely.

title: Entropy quantifies uncertainty
blocks: For a finite random variable X, entropy H(X) measures average uncertainty in bits. The logarithm is base 2.
Use the convention 0 log₂ 0 = 0, obtained by taking a limit. A certain outcome has entropy zero.
notes: Corrects the reference’s publication year for this information-theory paper: 1948, while the secrecy-systems paper is 1949. Entropy is distributional uncertainty, not a visual randomness score for a single string. The next coin examples fix the units and interpretation.

title: Coin examples: uncertainty decreases with bias
blocks: Let X be the coin outcome and let q = Pr[X = Heads]. Compare the same two-outcome space under three distributions.
take: q = 0.5 gives 1 bit; q = 0.7 gives about 0.881 bits; q = 1 gives 0 bits.
notes: Compare the three labeled bars at 1, 0.8812908992, and 0 bits, for fair/biased/certain coin. Explain a representative computation: -.7log2(.7)-.3log2(.3). A probability-one outcome contributes -1log2(1)=0; the impossible outcome contributes the limit 0.

title: Language: single letters and longer blocks differ
blocks: Entropy rate often estimated around 1–1.5 bits
Words, spelling, and context create dependencies. A single-letter entropy is not the same quantity as the long-text entropy rate.
notes: These English values are illustrative estimates, not universal constants or values from one specified fitted corpus. The key distinction is between one marginal H(P_i), a normalized block entropy, and the limiting rate. English text is neither independent nor uniform.

title: Define the entropy rate of a language model
blocks: Let Pᵢ be the random letter at position i in a language model. Joint block entropy includes dependencies between its letters.
H_L is measured in bits per letter. For the coming numerical illustration, assume H_L = 1.25; this is a model choice, not an exact property of English.
notes: H(P_1,...,P_n) is the entropy of the whole length-n vector using the same finite-variable definition. A stationary finite-alphabet model has a well-defined entropy rate. Avoid substituting a one-letter marginal estimate such as 4.19 where the calculation needs the rate 1.25.

title: Redundancy: unused uncertainty per letter
blocks: Let A be the 26-letter alphabet. Its maximum entropy per letter is hₘₐₓ; define D as redundancy in bits per letter and R_L as its fraction.
Under H_L = 1.25, this model is about 73% redundant. D and R_L are different quantities with different units.
notes: Use the same 1.25-bit rate in both the redundancy fraction and the next unicity calculation. D is in bits per letter; R_L is dimensionless. The reference mixed approximately 73% and 75%; this deck keeps one consistent numerical assumption.

title: Unicity distance is a model-based heuristic
blocks: As ciphertext grows, language structure can rule out candidate keys. Unicity distance estimates the length at which few plausible spurious keys are expected under the model.
H(K) is key entropy in bits and D is redundancy in bits per plaintext letter, so n₀ is measured in letters.
take: This is an information-theoretic heuristic, not an attack runtime or a guarantee for every message.
notes: Distinguish possible unique identification from efficient recovery. The estimate depends on a plaintext language model and cipher assumptions; it is not a sharp threshold below which all messages are safe or above which every key is recoverable.

title: Unicity estimate for a substitution cipher
blocks: For a uniformly selected alphabet permutation, the key space has 26! elements.
The estimate uses the same entropy-rate assumption as the preceding redundancy calculation.
notes: No 0.75 × 4.7 denominator is introduced: the actual denominator is log2(26)-1.25=3.450439718. The quotient is 25.614692777. It says nothing about how much computation a practical cryptanalyst needs.

title: Why 25.6 letters is not a universal threshold
blocks: Even known plaintext need not determine an entire substitution table. If only r distinct plaintext letters occur, mappings for the other 26 − r letters remain unconstrained by those pairs.
\text{Number of full permutation keys extending those pairs}=(26-r)!.
A long message made only of A cannot reveal all 26 mappings. Natural-language unicity estimates describe statistical expectations, not every possible string.
notes: This is a known-plaintext identifiability example, deliberately distinguished from the ciphertext-only heuristic. If r=1, there are 25! extensions even for a very long repeated-A message. For ciphertext-only language analysis there can be additional uncertainty. This reinforces the earlier lecture’s23observedletters/6extensions example.

title: Break / 10 minutes
blocks: Next: practical security, block-cipher rounds, and the Feistel construction.
take: 7:40 pm–7:50 pm • Resume at 7:50 pm
notes: Ten-minute break. The following section starts at the stated return time.

title: From perfect secrecy to practical security
blocks: OTP: ciphertext is independent of the message.
Attacks must exceed a specified resource budget.
No bound on the attacker’s computing power.
Assess time, memory, data, and attack model.
A fresh secret pad as long as the message.
A short reusable key, under usage limits.
A large key space is necessary for resisting exhaustive search. It does not establish security against other attacks.
take: Perfect secrecy is a statistical statement; practical security depends on a construction and an attack model.
notes: Do not call all information-theoretic security perfect secrecy: here perfect secrecy is the exact confidentiality property being contrasted.

title: Count keys before counting computers
blocks: Here k is the number of uniformly random key bits; R is the number of complete candidate-key tests per second.
take: These are hypothetical classical exhaustive-search costs, not measured hardware benchmarks.
notes: Assume enough known plaintext to reject incorrect keys. Mean cost is about half the key space; worst case is the full space.

title: Why FLOPS are not a cipher benchmark
blocks: A floating-point operation, a CPU clock cycle, and a complete DES or AES key test are different units of work.
An attack estimate must name the algorithm, implementation, hardware, memory, and data requirements.
Parallel hardware can accelerate search. Future improvements are uncertain; fixed doubling forecasts do not prove long-term security.
take: Measure the operation an attack actually performs.
notes: Replaces the original processor-price list and supercomputer league table. No live hardware ranking is needed.

title: The attacker’s information matters
blocks: A file has a predictable header.
The objective may be to recover the key or to decrypt additional messages. A useful cipher must resist known-plaintext attacks.
notes: A known message does not itself need to stay secret. The attack concerns the remaining protection.

title: Known plaintext: a useful contrast
blocks: ciphertext c XOR known plaintext p = pad k
This reveals the pad bits at those positions. Other fresh, independent pad bits remain unrevealed; known plaintext may still give contextual clues about the message.
For a block cipher, known plaintext and ciphertext give a test for a candidate key. They should not provide an efficient way to recover it.
take: Known plaintext defeats pad reuse; it does not defeat a correctly used OTP.
notes: Tie back to the reuse example, then distinguish fresh OTP positions from a block cipher’s deliberately reused key.

title: Kerckhoffs’ principle: put the secret in the key
blocks: Assume the attacker knows the cipher’s complete specification. Security should depend on the secrecy of the key.
Publishing a design enables independent analysis. It does not require attackers to share their discoveries.
Hidden designs can be recovered from software or hardware. Reverse engineering of MIFARE Classic’s Crypto1 is a historical example.
take: A public algorithm is compatible with a secret key.
notes: The original publication/cooperative-attacker claim is removed. Public scrutiny is useful but is not a proof of security.
source: Kerckhoffs (1883); MIFARE Classic / Crypto1 research published in 2008.

title: A block cipher selects a permutation
blocks: For each fixed key k, every n-bit input has a different n-bit output. This bijection makes decryption well defined.
take: n is the block size. The key size is a separate parameter.
notes: There are 2^n possible blocks, not n possible blocks. E is a family indexed by k.

title: Block size and key size answer different questions
blocks: Key length is not automatically security strength: three-key Triple DES does not provide 168-bit generic attack resistance.
notes: Only compare parameters. Do not introduce AES internals or modes in this lecture.

title: Build a complex permutation from simple rounds
blocks: An iterated cipher updates a state repeatedly. A key schedule derives a sequence of round keys from the master key.
take: Round keys are related outputs of one schedule, not independent fresh OTP pads.
notes: Define state as the current n-bit intermediate block. R_i denotes a round transformation, not the right half used in Feistel notation later.

title: Confusion and diffusion work together
blocks: Make relations among key, message, and ciphertext complex.
Spread local input influence across many state bits.
Routing followed by substitution; linear mixing.
A bit permutation only moves bits. Across rounds, it routes the output of one S-box into several later S-boxes.
take: Neither an S-box nor a wiring diagram alone guarantees a secure cipher.
notes: Avoid equating XOR by itself with nonlinear confusion. A deterministic bit permutation preserves the number of flipped bits.

title: Two useful round structures
blocks: Substitute small groups; mix or permute the state.
Split the state; transform one half and XOR into the other.
Invertible layers give an invertible cipher.
The full round is invertible even if its inner F is not.
Our next toy example illustrates the structure.
notes: This is the first definition of SPN. AES uses a substitution-permutation design but is not the toy network shown here.

title: Follow one 16-bit block through three rounds
blocks: Our plaintext is 1234 in hexadecimal. Each digit stands for four bits, so the four digits together form one 16-bit block.
take: For this example the four keys, in order, are K₀ = 3A94, K₁ = A94D, K₂ = 94D6, and K₃ = 4D63.
notes: Trace the arrows once. Each intermediate value replaces the preceding block. The S-box and four key values are teaching choices. Keep the first key and the plaintext on the board.

title: Round 1 · XOR the plaintext with the first key
blocks: Write the plaintext and K₀ as four groups of four bits. Compare matching bits. XOR gives 1 when the two bits differ and 0 when they match.
In the second group, 2 XOR A gives 0010 XOR 1010 = 1000. That is hex 8.
take: Read the four result groups from left to right to get 28A0.
notes: Align the first pair 0001 and 0011, then ask students to read their XOR, 0010. For the second pair, A is ten in decimal and 1010 in binary. Each XOR acts on corresponding bits independently.

title: Round 1 · Substitute each digit of 28A0
blocks: Use the same substitution table for each of the four digits. Find the input digit in the top row and copy the entry directly below it.
take: Join the four outputs in the order of the input digits. The new block is D36E.
notes: Begin with the digit 2. Find its column and read D below it. Ask the class to repeat that lookup for 8, A, and 0. Reading those four answers in message order gives D36E.

title: Round 1 · Where does the first output digit come from?
blocks: Expand D36E into bits and number them from 1 to 16, starting on the left. The permutation tells us to copy input positions 1, 5, 9, and 13 into the first four output slots.
take: The copied bits are 1001. In binary place values that is 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 9.
notes: Point separately at position 5 and at the 0 underneath it. Ask which of the two is copied. Students should answer 0. Then point to positions 9 and 13 and have them read their bits before forming 1001.

title: Round 1 · Copy the remaining bits in order
blocks: INPUT BITS GROUPED BY HEX DIGIT
Each row takes one bit from each input group. For the second row, take the second bit of D, then of 3, then of 6, then of E. This gives 1011, or hex B.
take: Reading the output digits in order gives 9B7C. This is the block that enters round 2.
notes: Before moving past row two, ask a student to find the bits at positions 2, 6, 10, and 14 on the preceding slide. Repeat for the third and fourth rows as needed. Every input position is used once.

title: Finish rounds 2 and 3, then apply the last key
blocks: Round 2 starts with 9B7C XOR A94D = 3231. Round 3 starts with 450E and ends after substitution at 9493.

9 XOR 4 = D    4 XOR D = 9    9 XOR 6 = F    3 XOR 3 = 0
9493 XOR 4D63 = D9F0
notes: For round 2 the S-box converts 3, 2, 3, 1 into 1, D, 1, 4. Use the same permutation to obtain 450E. In round 3 the permutation is omitted. To decrypt, first undo whitening with K₃, then undo the substitutions and earlier operations in reverse order.

title: Change one input bit and follow the difference
blocks: Change 1234 to 123C and keep the keys fixed. Only the last digit changes, from 4 (0100) to C (1100). That flips input bit 13.
take: In this example one input bit changes eight ciphertext bits. This illustrates diffusion across rounds.
notes: The permutation sends the changed bits to different S-boxes in the next round. The number of differences can then grow under substitution. The final XOR with the same key preserves the eight-bit difference.

title: What should a key schedule accomplish?
blocks: Derive all round keys reproducibly from a single secret key, so the receiver can generate the same sequence.
Aim to spread key-bit influence and avoid exploitable patterns, weak-key classes, and simple relations between round keys.
There is no universally optimal schedule. Its interaction with the round function must be analysed.
take: A complicated-looking schedule is not a substitute for cryptanalysis.
notes: DES will provide a concrete schedule using selection, rotation, and permutation. The toy round-key list was supplied directly.

title: Feistel: build an invertible round
take: Split into equal halves; transform the right half, XOR into the left half, then exchange their roles.
notes: Introduce Horst Feistel and the structural idea used by DES. The unchanged branch retains the information needed to undo the other branch. The drawn exchange is already part of the round equations; do not add an extra swap inside each round.

title: Write one round precisely
blocks: L and R are equal-length bit strings. Kᵢ is the subkey for round i; F produces a string the same length as a half-block.
The right half becomes the next left half. Its transformed value is mixed into the old left half using XOR.
take: The round is a transformation of the whole pair (L, R), not an inversion of F.
notes: Connect every symbol to the diagram. Distinguish the master key from a derived round key. F may have a different-size key input; the XOR requires its output to match the half-block length.

title: A four-bit-half example
take: Bitwise AND is non-invertible: with this key, both 0000 and 0001 map to 0000.
notes: Use F(R,K)=R AND K only for this tiny teaching model. Compute the four XOR positions aloud: 1010 XOR 0100 = 1110. This explicit non-invertible F demonstrates the structural property more clearly than an invertible addition example.

title: Undo a round without inverting F
take: The same F is evaluated again; XOR cancels the repeated value.
notes: The first inverse identity comes directly from the unchanged branch. Substitute that identity into the second, then cancel X XOR X. This proves invertibility for every F with the required input/output widths.

title: Two rounds: follow encryption and decryption
blocks: FINISH EACH DIRECTION BY SWAPPING HALVES
take: Decrypt with K₂, then K₁. See appendix A12–A13 for every AND, XOR, and final swap.
notes: Keep the toy function R AND K fixed in both directions. Distinguish the round state (L₂,R₂) from the externally serialized ciphertext (R₂,L₂). Give students three minutes to calculate the reverse steps using K₂ and then K₁ before discussing the result.

title: Break / 10 minutes
blocks: Next: follow a DES round, derive its round keys, and examine multiple encryption.
take: 8:50 pm–9:00 pm • Resume at 9:00 pm
notes: Ten-minute break. The following section starts at the stated return time.

title: DES: a historical standard
blocks: NIST standardizes AES as the successor.
NIST withdraws its Triple DES recommendation.
We study the design and its lessons. DES and Triple DES are historical constructions for new-encryption decisions.
take: DES shows how a bit-level construction becomes an efficiently reversible keyed permutation.
notes: Frame this as historical technical study, not deployment advice. DES originated in IBM research and was standardized by the US National Bureau of Standards, now NIST. AES details belong to a later lecture. TDEA withdrawal took effect on 1 January 2024.

title: DES parameters
take: The block length, effective key length, and subkey length are three different quantities.
notes: Prevent the common conflation of 64-bit block size with 64-bit security. For each fixed effective key, DES permutes the set of 64-bit blocks. The key schedule expands neither the independent key entropy nor the block size.

title: Why 64 key bits mean 56 secret bits
blocks: Each of the eight key bytes contains seven effective key bits and one odd-parity bit.
FIRST BYTE OF THE EXAMPLE KEY: HEX 13
The byte 00010011 has three 1s, so its parity is odd. Parity can detect some representation errors; it adds no secret-key strength.
take: PC1 discards the parity positions before generating round keys.
notes: Bit numbering in the DES tables is 1-based from the most significant bit. The parity positions are 8,16,…,64. The standard example key has odd parity in every byte. Changing only parity bits does not change DES encryption.

title: How does DES encrypt one block?
blocks: ONE BLOCK AND ITS MASTER KEY  •  HEXADECIMAL
take: Our first goal is to calculate the two halves leaving round 1. One hex digit represents four bits.
notes: Recall the two-round Feistel exercise on slide 57. DES repeats that same outer rule sixteen times. Trace the data across the diagram and pause at round 1. The example key includes the eight parity bits introduced on the preceding slide.

title: How to read the initial permutation
blocks: Read each row from left to right. Each entry names a plaintext bit to copy, counting from 1.
FIRST ROW  •  TAKE THE SECOND BIT OF EACH BYTE
take: The highlighted row gives 1100 1100 = CC in hex. Reading all eight rows gives CC00CCFFF0AAF0AA.
notes: Point to 58 in the highlighted row. The last byte EF occupies positions 57–64, so position 58 is its second bit. Move one cell right to 50. The preceding byte CD occupies positions 49–56, so position 50 is its second bit. Follow the remaining six cells from rightmost plaintext byte toward the left to get 11001100. Point to the next row for output bits 9–16. The entire result is split into L0 and R0 on the next slide.

title: What enters the first Feistel round?
blocks: APPLY IP, THEN SPLIT INTO TWO 32-BIT HALVES

IP output   CC00CCFFF0AAF0AA
Left  L₀    CC00CCFF
Right R₀    F0AAF0AA
USE THIS 48-BIT ROUND KEY FOR NOW
take: We can already write L₁ = F0AAF0AA. To calculate R₁, we need the value of F.
notes: Point to the first CC byte students have just calculated. The first eight hex digits make up L0 and the last eight make up R0. Treat K1 as given while working on the message. We derive this exact subkey after completing the round.

title: What is inside the DES round function?
blocks: In the toy example we used R AND K. DES keeps the Feistel rule and defines F with four operations. Follow the right half and the round key through them.
take: F returns 32 bits so its output can be XORed with the 32 bits of L₀.
notes: Point to the widths and the key entering at the XOR. Eight independent lookup tables shrink the result to 32 bits. The fixed permutation P is the last operation inside F. Leave the unchanged left input on the board until the end of the round.

title: Build the first six expansion bits
blocks: READ THE TWO ENDS OF THE RIGHT HALF
R₀ = F0AAF0AA     first byte F0 = 11110000     last digit A = 1010
The last bit is 0. The first five are 11110. Joining them in the order shown gives 011110, the first six bits of E(R₀).
take: Expansion builds eight six-bit groups from 32 bits. Neighbouring groups reuse boundary bits. The full E table is in A4.
notes: Read positions 32, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 aloud. Circle the last bit of A, then take the four bits of F and the leading zero of the next digit. The next group uses positions 4 through 9, so positions 4 and 5 appear again.

title: XOR six bits with six key bits
blocks: K₁ starts with hex 1B, or 0001 1011 in binary. Its first six bits are 000110. XOR gives 1 wherever the two input bits differ.
take: Split the 48-bit XOR result into eight groups of six. Send the first group, 011000, to S₁.
notes: Compare the six aligned columns on the left. Bit 4 is 1 in both inputs, so the output there is 0. The hex view on the right shows the same operation across all eight groups. Six-bit boundaries can fall in the middle of a hex digit.

title: Look up 011000 in the first S-box
take: S₁ returns decimal 5. Write it as 0101, the first four bits of the 32-bit S-box output.
notes: The two outside bits form a two-bit row number. The four middle bits form a four-bit column number. Rows and columns both start at zero. Follow the highlighted row and column to 5. Since this table maps 64 inputs to 16 values, different inputs can produce the same output.

title: Where does that first 5 go?
blocks: Each group goes to its own S-box, in order. Try S₂ on 010001. Which row and column would you use? The S₂ table is in A7.
JOIN THE EIGHT FOUR-BIT OUTPUTS FROM LEFT TO RIGHT
The 5 from S₁ becomes the first hex digit. The C from S₂ becomes the second. All eight together give 5C82B597.
take: See appendix A14 for all eight calculations, from the expansion and key bits to each S-box output.
notes: Let students answer before interpreting the output strip. For 010001, outer bits 01 select row 1 and inner bits 1000 select column 8. S2 gives 12 in decimal, written C in hex or 1100 in four bits.

title: Permute the 32 output bits
blocks: The P table uses the same copying rule as IP. In 5C82B597, bit 16 is the last bit of the fourth digit, 2 = 0010. Copy its 0 into output position 1.
FIRST OUTPUT DIGIT 0010 = 2  •  CONTINUE FOR ALL 32 POSITIONS
take: After P, the value of F(R₀, K₁) is 234AA9BB. It is ready to mix into the left half.
notes: To check another bit, select input position 20, the last bit of the fifth digit B = 1011. It supplies the 1 in output position 3. P just rearranges all 32 bits. The complete table appears in A4.

title: Put F back into the Feistel round
blocks: XOR F INTO THE OLD LEFT HALF
Check the first digit of R₁ by hand. Hex C XOR 2 gives 1100 XOR 0010 = 1110, or E.
take: Round 1 ends with (L₁, R₁) = (F0AAF0AA, EF4A6544). These two halves are the input to round 2.
notes: Ask which half was copied and which required the entire F calculation. Point back to the same two operations on slide 57. The output of F alone is not the right-half output of the round.

title: Retrace the calculation of F
blocks: Repeat boundary bits to make eight groups.
Mix the subkey into those groups.
Use a nonlinear six-bit to four-bit lookup.
Move those 32 bits to their next positions.
Read the formula from the inside out. If we kept R₀ and changed K₁, at which row could the result first change?
take: The expansion depends only on R₀. The subkey first affects the result at the XOR.
notes: Use the question as a pause before the key schedule. Ask a student to point to the 5 from S1 and the 2 that starts the final output of F. The S-boxes supply nonlinearity, while E and P are fixed public bit selections.

title: Where did the round key come from?
blocks: In round 1 we used K₁ = 1B02EFFC7072. Start with the master key and follow this separate calculation to reproduce those 48 bits.
take: The same 56 effective master-key bits determine all sixteen round keys.
notes: The message halves L and R are set aside here. C and D below are halves of the key. Expand the abbreviations: PC1 is Permuted Choice 1, and PC2 is Permuted Choice 2.

title: Select the 56 key bits with PC1
blocks: Permuted Choice 1 (PC1) reads the master key in a fixed order and skips the parity bit in each byte. Its first entry is 57. The last key byte is F1, or 11110001, so bit 57 is 1.
SPLIT THE PC1 OUTPUT AFTER SEVEN HEX DIGITS

Master key   133457799BBCDFF1
PC1 output   F0CCAAF556678F
Key halves   C₀ = F0CCAAF    D₀ = 556678F
take: Each key half contains 28 bits. The full PC1 and PC2 tables are in A5.
notes: Key positions 8, 16, …, 64 carry parity. PC1 selects all the remaining positions once and rearranges them. Ask how seven hex digits correspond to 28 bits. The first digit F of C0 starts with the 1 just identified.

title: Rotate each key half one place
blocks: In round 1, move the leftmost bit of each 28-bit half to its own right-hand end. Follow the separated bit in C₀.
ONE-BIT ROTATION OF THE LEFT KEY HALF
ROTATE THE RIGHT HALF BY THE SAME AMOUNT

C₀ F0CCAAF  →  C₁ E19955F
D₀ 556678F  →  D₁ AACCF1E
take: Round numbers 1, 2, 9 and 16 rotate by one place. The other rounds rotate by two, starting from the previous halves.
notes: Have students follow the leading 1 to the right end of C1. D0 rotates within its own 28 positions. Joining the halves before rotating would give a different result. A6 lists the shifts and every computed subkey.

title: Recover the six key bits we used
blocks: Join C₁ and D₁ to form a 56-bit string. Permuted Choice 2 (PC2) picks 48 positions from it. Read the first six entries exactly as we read the IP and E tables.
ROTATED KEY HALVES SIDE BY SIDE
take: The first six bits are 000110, exactly the bits we XORed with 011110 to enter S₁.
notes: Read the first copied bit from position 14 of the combined 56 bits. Complete the first six selections together. The remaining 42 selections follow the same rule. K1 is one 48-bit subkey derived from the original key.

title: Start round 2 with the output of round 1
blocks: Before calculating F again, which half of the round 2 output can you already write down?

L₂ = R₁ = EF4A6544
R₂ = L₁ XOR F(R₁, K₂) = F0AAF0AA XOR 3CAB87A3 = CC017709
take: Repeat this round rule through round 16, using the next subkey each time. Appendix A11 lists the sixteen output pairs.
notes: Ask for L2 before uncovering the last box. The class can now follow later rounds without manually performing another eight lookups. Verify that round 2 starts from the pair at the end of round 1 and consumes K2 from the same key schedule.

title: Finish encryption after round 16
blocks: SWAP THE HALVES, THEN APPLY THE FINAL PERMUTATION
The final permutation (FP) undoes the opening bit rearrangement. Its first entry is 40, so it copies bit 40 of the swapped block into ciphertext position 1.
take: The plaintext 0123456789ABCDEF encrypts to 85E813540F0AB405 with master key 133457799BBCDFF1.
notes: Point out the order of the two halves in the concatenation. FP is IP inverse, so it uses the full table in A3. Bits 33 to 40 of the swapped block form hex 43, ending in 1. This matches the leading bit of the ciphertext, which begins with hex 8.

title: Undo the last round first
blocks: Recall the two-round example on slide 57. There we started decryption with K₂. DES has sixteen rounds, so start with K₁₆.

Copy right      43423234
F(right, K₁₆)   C8C04F98
XOR into left   0A4CD995 XOR C8C04F98 = C28C960D
take: The first decryption round gives (R₁₅, L₁₅) = (43423234, C28C960D).
notes: IP undoes the FP just applied during encryption. The right half entering F is L16, equal to R15, so using K16 reproduces F = C8C04F98 from the last encryption round. XOR cancels it. Use A11 to compare the resulting pair with the round 15 pair in exchanged order.

title: Recover the original plaintext
blocks: USE THE SAME DES ROUNDS WITH THE SUBKEYS IN REVERSE

Encrypt   K₁,  K₂,  …, K₁₅, K₁₆
Decrypt   K₁₆, K₁₅, …, K₂,  K₁
AFTER ALL SIXTEEN DECRYPTION ROUNDS  •  HEX

Output pair   (F0AAF0AA, CC00CCFF)
After swap    CC00CCFFF0AAF0AA
After FP      0123456789ABCDEF
take: The last swap restores the two halves in their original order. FP returns them to their original plaintext bit positions.
notes: Compare the value after the swap with the IP output at the start. The same F, S-boxes, initial and final permutations work in both directions. Only the order of subkeys changes, as in the two-round Feistel example.

title: The effective key size became the problem
blocks: With a known plaintext/ciphertext pair, an attacker can test a candidate key by computing one block encryption.
In 1998, the EFF’s dedicated DES-cracking hardware recovered a challenge key in about 56 hours.
The historical response was to apply DES several times with more than one key.
take: Hardware and cost estimates age; the structural limitation is the small 56-bit key space.
notes: Retain the historical exhaustive-search lesson without presenting the old 2006 hardware budget as a current benchmark. A candidate match should be checked against additional data as needed. Multiple encryption must be analyzed rather than judged by the count of nominal key bits.

title: Double DES and the meet-in-the-middle idea
blocks: Store each middle value with its K₁, trying all 2⁵⁶ keys. Then try all 2⁵⁶ choices of K₂ from the ciphertext side and look for matches.
Use additional known pairs to reject false key-pair matches.
take: Two 56-bit keys do not automatically provide 112-bit security.
notes: Keep this to the equality and cost intuition; a detailed attack lecture is outside the scope. The memory estimate is enormous. A single 64-bit plaintext/ciphertext pair permits many key-pair candidates, so a table match is not by itself proof of the unique correct keys.

title: Triple DES uses encrypt–decrypt–encrypt
blocks: This historical EDE composition applies three DES transformations to the same 64-bit block.
take: If all three keys are equal, EDE collapses to ordinary DES: the middle inverse cancels one encryption.
notes: Read the composition from the innermost operation outward, matching the diagram from plaintext to ciphertext. EDE was chosen in part for compatibility with single-DES behavior when all keys coincide. The inverse and historical key options follow on the next page.

title: Triple DES: inverse, key options, and retirement
blocks: Three-key EDE has about 112-bit generic security, despite 168 bits of key material. The two-key option has additional historical weaknesses.
NIST withdrew its Triple DES (TDEA) recommendation on 1 January 2024. DES and Triple DES are unsuitable choices for new encryption.
take: The block size remains 64 bits; extra key material does not remove the data-volume limits of a small block.
notes: Separate nominal effective key material from achieved attack resistance. Do not label the two-key option as 112-bit secure just because it contains 112 independent key bits. The 64-bit block creates restrictive data-volume limits in common modes, which are covered later. TDEA stands for Triple Data Encryption Algorithm. NIST withdrawal concerns new cryptographic protection; processing previously protected data has separate transition guidance.

title: Three ideas to carry forward
blocks: With a uniform independent fresh pad, observing ciphertext does not change the message distribution.
A short key selects a permutation; security depends on the full design and the attacker’s resources.
Reversibility can survive a non-invertible inner function; a sound structure still needs adequate key and block sizes.
DES and Triple DES explain foundational design choices. Modern cipher design and message-encryption modes follow in later lectures.
notes: Use the last minutes for clarification and returning to the difference between a theorem of independence and a computational security assessment. The optional appendix is a reference, not material to rush through.

title: A1 / Conditional entropy for the key-size bound
blocks: For finite random variables X and Y, conditional entropy averages the uncertainty in X after observing Y. Sum only over positive-probability y.
Here H(X | Y = y) is the entropy of the conditional distribution. Joint and further-conditioned entropies use the same definition.
take: Z denotes any further finite observation. Conditioning cannot increase entropy on average.
notes: Preparation for the optional Shannon key-uncertainty bound. State the chain rule, nonnegativity, and H(X|Y)≤H(X); these are average statements, not inequalities for every individual observed value y. This appendix page is not needed to follow the main OTP proof.

title: A2 / Perfect secrecy requires enough key uncertainty
blocks: Let P, K, C be finite plaintext, key, and ciphertext variables. Assume exact decryption from K and C, and perfect secrecy.
H(P)=H(P\mid C)\le H(P,K\mid C)=H(K\mid C)\le H(K).
Therefore H(K) ≥ H(P). An n-bit uniform OTP key has H(K) = n; equality with message entropy occurs when P is also uniform on all n-bit strings.
notes: The chain rule and exact decryption make H(P,K|C)=H(K|C). The first inequality adds the nonnegative conditional uncertainty of K after P,C; the last uses conditioning-reduces-entropy. Do not infer that a biased message source always has H(P)=n or that this entropy inequality alone constructs a usable secure cipher.

title: A3 / DES reference / initial and final permutations
blocks: Read each table left to right, top to bottom. Each entry specifies the 1-based input position copied to the next output position.
take: Positions are numbered from the most significant input bit. FP exactly inverts IP.
notes: Complete FIPS 46-3 wiring tables. These are retained for independent calculation and implementation checking, not memorization.

title: A4 / DES reference / expansion E and permutation P
blocks: E repeats selected boundary bits. P is a permutation of the 32 concatenated S-box output bits.
take: The table values are input bit positions, not S-box outputs or numeric additions.
notes: E has 48 entries selected from 32 input positions; P has each position 1 through 32 exactly once.

title: A5 / DES reference / PC1 and PC2
blocks: PC1 omits parity positions 8,16,…,64. PC2 reads the concatenated, already rotated halves Cᵢ ∥ Dᵢ.
take: These are key-schedule selections. They are different from the data-path IP and P tables.
notes: Key representation has 64 bits, schedule halves have 28 bits each, and each selected subkey has 48 bits. Complete tables are taken directly from the shared verified example module.

title: A6 / DES reference / rotations and all sixteen subkeys
take: Master key 133457799BBCDFF1. Rotations are cumulative within each 28-bit half.
notes: Every key is printed as 12 hexadecimal digits, representing 48 bits. A two-column presentation preserves all 16 rows without shrinking the type excessively.

title: A7 / DES reference / S-boxes S1 and S2
take: For six-bit input b₁b₂b₃b₄b₅b₆, use outer bits b₁b₆ for the row and inner bits b₂b₃b₄b₅ for the column.
notes: Each entry is a decimal number 0–15; encode it as a four-bit output. All eight distinct DES S-boxes are retained. Row and column indices are zero-based.

title: A8 / DES reference / S-boxes S3 and S4
take: For six-bit input b₁b₂b₃b₄b₅b₆, use outer bits b₁b₆ for the row and inner bits b₂b₃b₄b₅ for the column.
notes: Each entry is a decimal number 0–15; encode it as a four-bit output. All eight distinct DES S-boxes are retained. Row and column indices are zero-based.

title: A9 / DES reference / S-boxes S5 and S6
take: For six-bit input b₁b₂b₃b₄b₅b₆, use outer bits b₁b₆ for the row and inner bits b₂b₃b₄b₅ for the column.
notes: Each entry is a decimal number 0–15; encode it as a four-bit output. All eight distinct DES S-boxes are retained. Row and column indices are zero-based.

title: A10 / DES reference / S-boxes S7 and S8
take: For six-bit input b₁b₂b₃b₄b₅b₆, use outer bits b₁b₆ for the row and inner bits b₂b₃b₄b₅ for the column.
notes: Each entry is a decimal number 0–15; encode it as a four-bit output. All eight distinct DES S-boxes are retained. Row and column indices are zero-based.

title: A11 / DES reference / all sixteen round states
take: The state is (Lᵢ,Rᵢ) after each round. Preoutput is R₁₆ ∥ L₁₆ before FP; ciphertext is 85E813540F0AB405.
notes: Initial halves are L0=CC00CCFF and R0=F0AAF0AA. The full trace is generated from the same known-answer example; preserve leading zeros in the eight-digit half-block displays.

title: A12 / Feistel by hand / encryption
blocks: Split the plaintext 10101100 into L = 1010 and R = 1100. Read each round down its column. Work one bit at a time. AND gives 1 when both bits are 1. XOR gives 1 when the bits differ.
2. Copy R to the new left
FINAL SWAP  •  WRITE THE RIGHT HALF FIRST, THEN THE LEFT
notes: AND gives 1 when both input bits are 1. XOR gives 1 when the bits differ. The symbol || joins the two four-bit halves. In each round calculate F from the input right half and use the input left half for the XOR.

title: A13 / Feistel by hand / decryption
blocks: Split the ciphertext 10001110 into L = 1000 and R = 1110. Apply the same round rule, using K₂ first and K₁ second.
2. Copy R to the new left
FINAL SWAP  •  WRITE THE RIGHT HALF FIRST, THEN THE LEFT
notes: Check the pair after the first reverse round against the first encryption round. Their halves appear in opposite order. The final swap gives the original plaintext, 10101100.

title: A14 / Round 1 / all eight S-box calculations
sub: Read across each row. XOR the two six-bit groups, then look up the result in that row’s S-box.
take: Join the outputs from S1 to S8 in order. 0101 1100 1000 0010 1011 0101 1001 0111 = 5C82B597 (hex).
notes: The first and sixth bits of the XOR result give the row. The four bits between them give the column. Both indices start at zero. Use the S-box tables in A7–A10 to check each four-bit output.
